questions.q: Why do quant models typically work with returns instead of raw prices?
options: Returns are always positive, which simplifies the math
Raw price series are non-stationary, while returns are far closer to stationary
Exchanges only publish return data, not price data
Returns eliminate the need for any statistical testing
questions.explain: Raw prices drift in mean and variance over time (non-stationary), which violates assumptions behind most time series models. Returns approximate stationarity much better.

questions.q: Which property makes simple returns the right choice for computing a portfolio's overall return from its holdings?
options: Time additivity
They are always smaller in magnitude than log returns
Cross-sectional (portfolio) additivity — the weighted average of simple returns equals the portfolio return
They are computed using natural logarithms
questions.explain: Simple returns are cross-sectionally additive: a portfolio's simple return is the weighted sum of its holdings' simple returns. Log returns do not have this property.

questions.q: A stock's log return over 5 trading days is the sum of its 5 daily log returns. What property does this demonstrate?
options: Cross-sectional additivity
Mean reversion
Time additivity
Stationarity
questions.explain: Log returns are time-additive: the multi-period log return equals the sum of the one-period log returns, ln(P_t/P_(t-k)) = r_t + r_(t-1) + ... + r_(t-k+1).

questions.q: In pandas, which pair of operations correctly computes log returns from a price Series called `prices`?
options: prices.pct_change() alone
np.log(prices).diff(), equivalently np.log(prices / prices.shift(1))
prices.cumsum()
prices.diff() without any log transform
questions.explain: Log returns are the difference of the log-transformed price series: ln(P_t) - ln(P_(t-1)), computed as np.log(prices).diff().

questions.q: To recover cumulative growth from a series of log returns, what is the correct approach?
options: Sum the log returns, then take the exponential of that sum
Sum the log returns and stop — no further transform needed
Multiply the log returns together directly
Average the log returns
questions.explain: Log returns compound additively, so summing them gives the cumulative log return; exponentiating that sum converts it back into cumulative simple growth, exp(sum(r_1...r_n)).
